“How do we run our AI agents in production at scale?” is the question every customer eventually asks. It comes bundled with several questions. How do we handle thousands of concurrent user requests securely and confidently? How do we make sure the agents stay reliable under real traffic instead of failing silently? How do we know if an agent still meets the quality and safety standards it passed during testing? What are agent security best practices? Should that be deterministic or non-deterministic? And many more. A proof-of-concept answers none of these, because it is built to show the agent model can do the task, not to survive production traffic, cost pressure, and security review.

That gap between a working prototype and a system that runs reliably, securely, frugally and responsibly at scale, is where most agentic AI initiatives stall, and it is rarely the model’s fault. Every team building an agent tends to rebuild the same scaffolding from scratch: its own routing logic, its own guardrails, its own observability, all applied after the fact rather than built in from the start. The teams need a shared, production-ready architecture that every agent can build on.

This post walks through a seven-layer composable reference architecture designed to take multi-agent AI applications from prototype to production scale.

Composable architecture

The Pluggable Agentic AI Framework is a reference architecture for multi-agent applications organized into seven layers, each with a distinct responsibility and a stable contract. The services and technologies shown in each layer reflect the reference implementation, not mandatory choices. Organizations can substitute alternatives that align with their existing infrastructure and requirements. Together, these layers offer a blueprint for building, securing, and operating agentic AI applications at production scale.

Figure 1: The seven layers of the Pluggable Agentic AI Framework

Data and Knowledge is the foundation of Agentic AI. An agent is only as good as the data it can access. Whether an agent is checking out a healthcare formulary, tracking inventory, or interpreting a compliance rule, it needs relevant, up-to-date information to answer correctly. This layer owns retrieval, embeddings, and access to structured and unstructured data through a clear contract and protocol: accept a query and return the most relevant information that acts as context for an agent. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base, Vector Engine for Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, Amazon S3 Vectors and Amazon DynamoDB are example building blocks for this foundation.

Model and Inference choices should be driven by configuration, not hardwired into agent or application logic. Use smaller, faster models for simple tasks and larger models for requests that require more nuanced reasoning. It is important to conduct a thorough model evaluation for the use case you are building with realistic and representative business data. A model routing layer keeps AI agents decoupled from the model hosting environment and provider-specific APIs by relying on a consistent request-and-response contract. A proxy such as LiteLLM provides a common interface across providers, so you can switch models based on your evaluations without rewriting application logic.

Orchestration determines how work is distributed, and choosing the right approach is critical. For straightforward tasks, use a single agent to handle the work from end to end. For complex, cross-domain workflows, use a supervisor to delegate specialist agents, each scoped to a specific capability and tied to a specific set of tools. Avoid building one agent that does everything. As tools, instructions, and context accumulate, the context window grows, latency increases, and accuracy can suffer. Tool sprawl sets in, which can push agents beyond their intended boundaries, leading to unintended actions and security breaches. Splitting responsibilities keeps each agent’s context focused and makes latency more predictable. You can also test each agent’s behavior, scale it, and define its security model independently. Enforce bounded autonomy: specialists should execute strictly within the tools they have been granted, and nothing more.

In addition to decomposing into specific specialists and setting its boundary, decouple the specialist agents from the supervisor agents. Allow the supervisor to discover the specialists from a centralized agent registry and invoke them through a standardized protocol like MCP (Model Context Protocol) and A2A (Agent to Agent). Maintain a centralized agent registry that catalogs every agent’s tools, skills, and owner. This gives your organization the visibility it needs for governance at scale, increases the velocity of AI agent implementation through reusability, and avoids the cost of repetitive development. Consider using Strands Agents for specialists, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness for the orchestrator, AWS Agent Registry and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway for centralized discovery and routing.

Security and Guardrails should be a primary concern, built into the design from day one. Agentic AI exposes organizations to a new class of risks that conventional security frameworks were not built to address, from prompt injection and tool misuse to memory and data poisoning. Treat all external content as untrusted by default. Authenticate every request, whether it comes from a user, another agent, or an automated workflow, through a service like Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity. Then use fine-grained access control to determine whether each tool call is permitted before execution. Grant agents temporary, scoped credentials instead of persistent secrets. On the data-protection side, mask sensitive data like PHI (Personal Health Information) and PII (Personally Identifiable Information) in agent and tool requests and responses, so that sensitive customer information does not appear in agent outputs or lingers in memory. For accountability, capture every significant decision in a tamper-evident audit trail, route high-impact actions through a human approval gate, and deploy circuit breakers to halt anomalous behavior before it can escalate. Consider using Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for user inputs, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity and Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for authentication and access control, along with AWS Security and governance controls to bring defense-in-depth security.

Application is where the end-user experience lives, whether that is a chat interface, an API surface, or an embedded widget. Keep this layer intentionally thin. Its only responsibilities should be presenting the conversation and passing requests to the orchestration layer beneath it. Resist the urge to embed business logic here. The cleaner the separation, the more easily you can iterate on the user experience without destabilizing the backend. A decision model can sit at this boundary as a fast, inexpensive check: in one call it scores whether a request is in scope, needs a human, or is urgent, returning probabilities instead of free text. Your code acts on those scores with simple thresholds, answering off-topic requests directly and flagging escalations, so the full agentic loop runs only when it adds value. When building the application layer, think about what would be needed for another AI agent to consume and interact with your AI agents along with humans. Build your external interfaces accordingly.

Observability should watch every layer from day one, not after the first incident. Along with the logs and metrics, end-to-end agent traces are critical to measure whether the agent performed its task correctly. Along with the trace, collect cost and token usage per request, time to first token, whether the call is secure, and surface dashboards for latency, error rates, and spend before you go live. Proactive monitoring is cheaper than reactive firefighting. Consider using Amazon CloudWatch with OpenTelemetry along with Amazon CloudWatch Omni for tracing and metrics to get comprehensive visibility across your stack.

Agentic Operations closes the loop with continuous evaluation, so set it up from day one. Score every production session for groundedness, accuracy, and safety, and put a regression gate in place to catch quality drops before they reach customers. Without this, you only know the agent worked at launch. With it, you can prove it still works after every subsequent release. Consider using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations for scoring and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore optimization for continuous performance tuning.

Reference implementation for a retail customer support agent

Figure 2: Functional flow of the retail customer support reference implementation

To bring the architecture to life, the framework includes a ready-to-run reference implementation based on a retail customer support scenario covering order status and refund eligibility. We chose this use case because it exercises every layer of the stack while remaining intuitive enough for a team to follow and adapt to their own needs.

A supervisor agent receives a customer’s refund request and delegates to an Order agent and a Refund agent, each a specialist with a scoped set of tools. The Order agent looks up delivery and purchase details from Amazon DynamoDB. The Refund agent retrieves tier-based policy rules from a knowledge base and calculates eligibility using the delivery date, the current date, and the customer’s loyalty tier. Every one of these calls passes through the AgentCore Gateway, which enforces fine-grained access control before a tool executes with Policy in AgentCore, and every call is traced end-to-end through the observability layer, so when a calculation goes wrong, the trace shows exactly which layer and which decision point caused it.

Anyone building a similar supervisor-and-specialist pattern can clone the reference implementation and swap in their own domain logic layer by layer.

Why pluggability matters as much as the layers themselves

The value of a seven-layer architecture lies not only in how it separates responsibilities, but in how quickly each layer can evolve. Pluggability makes that possible. Stable contracts at layer boundaries, from identity checks and access policies to telemetry interfaces, let you change the underlying technology without redesigning the rest of the stack. Essentially, take an architecture-first approach to building agentic AI systems rather than a technology-driven approach.

The framework puts this into practice by demonstrating pluggability through integrations with third-party providers across the layers: model and hosting providers at the inference layer, search capabilities at the orchestration layer, decision APIs at the application layer, guardrails at the security layer, and agent tracing and monitoring solutions at the observability layer alongside business value and cost tracking. It supports industry-standard providers at each layer, so you can compose solutions that meet your specific requirements.

For enterprises, flexibility protects existing investments. Teams can retain the observability, security, and inference tools they already trust, fill gaps where needed, and adopt new capabilities incrementally. The architecture provides a consistent foundation without requiring every technology decision to come from the same vendor.

Conclusion

A working prototype proves what an agent can do. A well-designed architecture determines whether your enterprise can depend on it. Moving to AI operations means designing security, governance, visibility, cost controls, reliability, and adaptability into the design from day one, not adding them after the system is built.

The Pluggable Agentic AI Framework brings those concerns into an architecture with a clear principle: build a stable foundation without locking every technology choice in place. Models will change. Tools will evolve. Business requirements will shift. Your architecture should make those changes manageable, not turn each one into a rebuild.

Put that principle into practice. Start with the Workshop Studio experience, explore the public sample repository, and use the hands-on implementation as a starting point for your own architecture. It is not a substitute for production security hardening, testing, and review.

Build the capabilities you need today and the flexibility you will need tomorrow.

About the authors

translation.html:
“如何在生产环境中大规模运行 AI 智能体？”这是每位客户最终都会提出的问题。随之而来的还有一系列问题。如何安全、有把握地处理数千个并发用户请求？如何确保智能体在真实流量下保持可靠，而不是悄无声息地出错？如何判断智能体是否仍然符合测试时达到的质量和安全标准？智能体安全有哪些最佳实践？应该采用确定性方式还是非确定性方式？诸如此类的问题还有很多。概念验证无法回答其中任何一个问题，因为它的目的是展示智能体模型能够完成任务，而不是检验其能否经受住生产流量、成本压力和安全审查。

从可用的原型，到能够大规模可靠、安全、节约且负责任地运行的系统，两者之间的差距，是大多数智能体 AI 项目停滞不前的地方，而问题很少出在模型本身。每个构建智能体的团队往往都会从头重建同一套基础支撑：自己的路由逻辑、自己的防护机制、自己的可观测性，而且都是事后补上，而非从一开始就融入系统。团队需要一套共享的、可用于生产环境的架构，让每个智能体都能在此基础上构建。

本文将介绍一套由七层组成的可组合参考架构，旨在帮助多智能体 AI 应用从原型走向生产级规模。

可组合架构

可插拔智能体 AI 框架（Pluggable Agentic AI Framework）是一套多智能体应用参考架构，分为七层，每层都有明确的职责和稳定的契约。各层展示的服务和技术来自参考实现，并非强制选择。组织可以根据现有基础设施和需求替换为其他方案。这些层共同构成了一份蓝图，用于以生产级规模构建、保护和运行智能体 AI 应用。

图 1：可插拔智能体 AI 框架的七层结构

数据与知识是智能体 AI 的基础。智能体的能力取决于它能访问的数据。无论智能体是在查阅医疗药品目录、跟踪库存，还是解读合规规则，都需要相关且最新的信息才能正确回答。这一层负责检索、嵌入，以及通过明确的契约和协议访问结构化与非结构化数据：接收查询，返回最相关的信息，为智能体提供上下文。Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base、Vector Engine for Amazon OpenSearch Serverless、Amazon S3 Vectors 和 Amazon DynamoDB 都是构建这一基础层的组件示例。

模型与推理的选择应由配置驱动，而不是硬编码在智能体或应用逻辑中。简单任务使用更小、更快的模型，需要更细致推理的请求则使用更大的模型。针对正在构建的用例，使用真实且具有代表性的业务数据进行全面的模型评估十分重要。模型路由层依靠一致的请求与响应契约，使 AI 智能体与模型托管环境及提供商特有的 API 解耦。LiteLLM 这样的代理可以为不同提供商提供统一接口，让你根据评估结果切换模型，无须重写应用逻辑。

编排决定工作如何分配，选择合适的方法至关重要。对于简单任务，使用单个智能体从头到尾处理。对于复杂的跨领域工作流，使用主管智能体向专业智能体分派任务，每个专业智能体都限定于某项特定能力，并绑定一组特定工具。避免构建一个包办所有事情的智能体。随着工具、指令和上下文不断累积，上下文窗口会增大，延迟会上升，准确性也可能受到影响。工具会逐渐泛滥，可能把智能体推到预期边界之外，导致非预期操作和安全事件。拆分职责可以让每个智能体的上下文保持聚焦，也让延迟更可预测。你还可以独立测试每个智能体的行为、扩展其规模，并定义其安全模型。要落实有边界的自主性：专业智能体必须严格在获准使用的工具范围内执行，不能越界。

除了拆分出具体的专业智能体并设定其边界，还应将专业智能体与主管智能体解耦。让主管智能体通过集中式智能体注册表发现专业智能体，并通过 MCP（模型上下文协议）和 A2A（智能体间通信）等标准化协议调用它们。维护一个集中式智能体注册表，记录每个智能体的工具、技能和负责人。这能为组织提供大规模治理所需的可见性，通过复用加快 AI 智能体的实施速度，并避免重复开发的成本。可以考虑使用 Strands Agents 构建专业智能体，使用 Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness 构建编排器，并使用 AWS Agent Registry 和 Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway 实现集中式发现与路由。

安全与防护机制应是首要关注点，从第一天起就融入设计。智能体 AI 让组织面临一类新的风险，从提示注入、工具滥用，到记忆和数据投毒，而传统安全框架并非为应对这些风险而设计。默认将所有外部内容视为不可信。无论请求来自用户、其他智能体还是自动化工作流，都要通过 Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity 这样的服务对其进行身份验证。随后，在执行前使用细粒度访问控制判断每次工具调用是否获准。向智能体授予限定作用范围的临时凭证，而非长期有效的密钥。在数据保护方面，应对智能体和工具请求与响应中的 PHI（个人健康信息）和 PII（个人身份信息）等敏感数据进行脱敏，防止敏感客户信息出现在智能体输出中或残留在记忆里。为确保可追责，应将每项重要决策记录到可检测篡改的审计轨迹中，让高影响操作经过人工审批关卡，并部署熔断机制，在异常行为升级之前将其停止。可以考虑使用 Amazon Bedrock Guardrails 处理用户输入，使用 Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity 和 Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore 实现身份验证与访问控制，并结合 AWS 的安全与治理控制措施，构建纵深防御。

应用层承载最终用户体验，无论是聊天界面、API 接口，还是嵌入式组件。应有意让这一层保持精简。它的职责应仅限于呈现对话，以及将请求传递给下方的编排层。不要把业务逻辑嵌入这一层。职责划分越清晰，就越容易在不影响后端稳定性的情况下迭代用户体验。可以在这一边界部署一个决策模型，进行快速、低成本的检查：通过一次调用，对请求是否在范围内、是否需要人工介入、是否紧急进行评分，并返回概率而非自由文本。代码通过简单阈值根据这些分数采取行动，直接回应偏离主题的请求，并标记需要升级处理的情况，让完整的智能体循环仅在能创造价值时运行。构建应用层时，要考虑除了人类之外，另一个 AI 智能体使用你的 AI 智能体并与之交互需要什么，并据此构建外部接口。

可观测性应从第一天起覆盖每一层，而不是等到第一次事故之后。除了日志和指标，端到端智能体追踪对于衡量智能体是否正确完成任务也至关重要。在收集追踪信息的同时，还应收集每次请求的成本和 token 用量、首个 token 的响应时间，以及调用是否安全，并在上线前提供展示延迟、错误率和支出的仪表板。主动监控的成本低于被动救火。可以考虑结合使用 Amazon CloudWatch、OpenTelemetry 和 Amazon CloudWatch Omni 进行追踪与指标监测，全面掌握整个技术栈的运行情况。

智能体运营通过持续评估形成闭环，因此应从第一天起建立。对每个生产环境会话的依据充分性、准确性和安全性进行评分，并设置回归检查关卡，在质量下降影响客户之前将其发现。没有这些措施，你只知道智能体在上线时能够正常工作。有了这些措施，你就能证明它在之后每次发布后仍然能够正常工作。可以考虑使用 Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations 进行评分，使用 Amazon Bedrock AgentCore optimization 持续调优性能。

零售客户支持智能体的参考实现

图 2：零售客户支持参考实现的功能流程

为让这套架构落地，框架提供了一个可直接运行的参考实现，以零售客户支持为场景，涵盖订单状态和退款资格。我们选择这一用例，是因为它能覆盖技术栈的每一层，同时又足够直观，方便团队理解并根据自身需求进行调整。

主管智能体接收客户的退款请求，并将任务分派给订单智能体和退款智能体，两者都是配有一组限定作用范围工具的专业智能体。订单智能体从 Amazon DynamoDB 查询配送和购买详情。退款智能体从知识库检索基于会员等级的政策规则，并根据配送日期、当前日期和客户的忠诚会员等级计算退款资格。每一次调用都经过 AgentCore Gateway，由它借助 Policy in AgentCore 在工具执行前实施细粒度访问控制；每次调用也都会通过可观测性层进行端到端追踪。因此，当计算出错时，追踪信息能够准确显示是哪个层、哪个决策点导致了问题。

任何构建类似主管与专业智能体模式的人，都可以克隆该参考实现，并逐层替换为自己的领域逻辑。

为什么可插拔性与各层本身同样重要

七层架构的价值不仅在于如何划分职责，还在于每一层能以多快的速度演进。可插拔性让这一点成为可能。从身份检查和访问策略，到遥测接口，层与层边界上的稳定契约，让你可以更换底层技术，而无须重新设计技术栈的其他部分。归根结底，构建智能体 AI 系统应采取架构优先的方法，而非技术驱动的方法。

该框架通过在各层集成第三方提供商来展示可插拔性，将这一理念付诸实践：推理层的模型与托管提供商、编排层的搜索能力、应用层的决策 API、安全层的防护机制，以及可观测性层的智能体追踪与监控方案，同时还包括业务价值与成本跟踪。它在每一层都支持符合行业标准的提供商，让你能够组合出满足特定需求的解决方案。

对于企业而言，灵活性可以保护现有投资。团队可以保留已经信赖的可观测性、安全和推理工具，按需补齐缺口，并逐步采用新能力。这套架构提供了一致的基础，无须让每一项技术选择都来自同一家供应商。

结论

一个可用的原型证明了智能体能做什么。一套设计良好的架构则决定了企业能否依赖它。迈向 AI 运营，意味着从第一天起就将安全、治理、可见性、成本控制、可靠性和适应性融入设计，而不是等系统建好后再补上。

可插拔智能体 AI 框架将这些关注点纳入架构，并遵循一个明确原则：构建稳定的基础，同时不锁死每一项技术选择。模型会改变，工具会演进，业务需求会变化。你的架构应让这些变化变得可控，而不是让每一次变化都变成一次重建。

将这一原则付诸实践。从 Workshop Studio 体验入手，探索公开示例代码仓库，并以动手实践的实现作为构建自身架构的起点。它不能替代生产环境的安全加固、测试和审查。

构建今天所需的能力，以及明天所需的灵活性。

关于作者
